questions.title: Basis of the Gram-positive / Gram-negative distinction
questions.question: The difference between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria resides in the:

explanations.A: Correct. The Gram reaction is a cell-wall stain: Gram-positive bacteria retain the crystal-violet-iodine complex because their wall is a thick, multilayered peptidoglycan sheet, while Gram-negative bacteria decolorise and take up the safranin counterstain because their wall is a thin peptidoglycan layer covered by an outer lipopolysaccharide membrane. It is this difference in wall architecture, not any other structure, that the stain is actually reading, which is why Gram reaction and wall structure are taught as the same fact.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bacteria have no true membrane-bound nucleus at all (that is what makes them prokaryotes), so the nucleus cannot be the structure the Gram stain distinguishes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cytoplasmic membrane lies beneath the cell wall in both groups and is not itself stained differently by the Gram method; it is the wall external to it that differs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mesosomes are cytoplasmic-membrane invaginations found to varying degrees in many bacteria and are not the structural basis the Gram stain distinguishes.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ribosomes are 70S in essentially all bacteria regardless of Gram reaction, so they cannot account for the staining difference.

questions.subtopic: Bacterial cell wall and Gram stain
questions.learning_objective: State that the Gram-positive/Gram-negative distinction is a cell-wall difference, not a difference in the membrane, nucleus, mesosomes or ribosomes.

field_notes.mint: find-existing.mjs run for "gram positive gram negative cell wall" and "gram" -- the closest existing records (CON-INF-0DD46C0FD80938 Gram-negative wall composition, CON-INF-7E3B831D71A008 teichoic acid) describe wall COMPOSITION per Gram type, not the more basic fact this stem tests (that the wall, as opposed to nucleus/membrane/mesosomes/ribosomes, is what the stain reads) -- minted a new umbrella concept rather than overloading either compositional record.

questions.title: Sporing (endospore-forming) bacterial genus
questions.question: Which of the following is a sporing bacterium?

explanations.A: Correct. Bacillus (together with Clostridium) is one of the two medically important genera able to form dormant, highly resistant endospores under adverse conditions such as heat, drying or nutrient depletion, allowing the organism to survive until conditions improve and then germinate back into a vegetative cell. This spore-forming ability is a key identification feature and also underlies the extra decontamination measures (autoclaving rather than simple boiling or disinfection) needed to reliably kill Bacillus and Clostridium species.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Helicobacter is a Gram-negative, curved, non-spore-forming organism (classically H. pylori, associated with peptic ulcer disease).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Campylobacter is likewise a Gram-negative, curved, non-spore-forming enteric pathogen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Staphylococci are Gram-positive cocci but do not form endospores.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Streptococci are also Gram-positive cocci without spore-forming ability.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Bacillus (with Clostridium) as the medically important endospore-forming bacterial genus.

field_notes.reuse: Reuses live concept CON-INF-3E6590C8AC2166 ('Bacillus and Clostridium can form dormant highly resistant non-replicating endospores'), status under review, live in server/data/medical-library-v1.json with working article ART-INF-TOP-1181606D78 ('General Bacteriology', in review). questions.title: Composition of the bacterial genome
questions.question: The bacterial genome consists of a:

options.A: Haploid circular DNA associated with histone protein.
options.B: Diploid circular DNA without histone protein.
options.D: Circular DNA associated with histone protein and a plasmid.
options.E: Haploid circular DNA inside a nuclear envelope and plasmid outside.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The bacterial chromosome is not associated with histone proteins; histone packaging is a eukaryotic feature.
explanations.B: Correct per this bank's printed key. Standard teaching describes the bacterial genome as a single haploid (one copy) circular dsDNA molecule, free of histone proteins, lying in the nucleoid with no surrounding nuclear envelope -- closer to option C than to B, since bacteria are ordinarily taught as haploid rather than diploid. This bank's own answer table nonetheless marks B as the key; the printed key is followed here as the source's stated answer, with the standard-teaching discrepancy flagged rather than silently corrected.
explanations.C: Incorrect per the printed key, though this is the option that most closely matches standard textbook teaching (haploid circular DNA, no histone, no plasmid implied) -- see the note on option B.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The bacterial chromosome does not carry histone protein, and a plasmid, when present, is a separate, smaller, dispensable circular DNA molecule rather than part of the chromosome itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bacteria have no nuclear envelope around their chromosome; the DNA lies free in the cytoplasm as the nucleoid.

questions.learning_objective: State the standard description of the bacterial genome (haploid circular DNA, no histone, no nuclear envelope) and recognise this bank's printed key as inconsistent with that standard teaching.

field_notes.keySource: render-verified, p.28; the letter itself (B) is confirmed correct off the render, but the underlying fact is flagged as inconsistent with standard microbiology teaching -- see doubt note below
field_notes.mint: find-existing.mjs run for "bacterial genome haploid" -- no hit, safe to create.
field_notes.doubt: AUTHOR DOUBT, not silently corrected: standard teaching holds the bacterial genome is HAPLOID circular DNA without histone (closest to this stem's option C), not diploid. This bank's printed key nonetheless marks B ('Diploid circular DNA without histone protein'). Printed key followed per lane rule; flagged for whoever reviews this cluster.

questions.title: Enzyme used to cut recipient DNA in recombinant DNA technology
questions.question: Which of the following enzymes are used to cut the recipient DNA?

explanations.A: Correct. Restriction endonucleases are the bacterial enzymes used in recombinant DNA technology to cut both donor and recipient (vector) DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences; it is this internal, sequence-specific cutting -- not random or end-directed cutting -- that lets the two DNA molecules be spliced together at matching sites. Because the enzyme cuts only at its specific recognition sequence rather than randomly, it leaves predictable, reproducible fragment ends that can be matched to a similarly cut donor DNA fragment for ligation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Exonucleases degrade DNA progressively from a free end rather than cutting at an internal recognition site, so they are not the enzyme used to open recipient DNA for cloning.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ligases join (seal) DNA fragments together after cutting, acting at the opposite step of the cloning process from the one this question asks about.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Polymerases synthesise new DNA strands; they do not cut existing DNA.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Helicases unwind the DNA double helix ahead of replication or transcription; they do not cut DNA.

questions.learning_objective: Identify restriction endonucleases as the enzymes that cut recipient/vector DNA at specific sequences in recombinant DNA technology.

field_notes.reuse: Reuses pending concept CON-FND-C444D428BE3E1D ('Restriction endonucleases are bacterial enzymes that recognise and cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences...'), docs/import-ready/concept/ASU-MBG-gene-therapy-concepts.md, exact functional match. Article ART-FND-GENE-THERAPY-AND-RECOMBINANT-DNA-TECHNOLOGY confirmed present in the same batch.

questions.title: Structure present in Gram-negative but not Gram-positive bacteria
questions.question: Which one of the following structures is present in Gram negative but not in Gram positive bacteria:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Peptidoglycan is present in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative walls, just in very different amounts (a thick multilayer in Gram-positives, a thin single layer in Gram-negatives).
explanations.B: Correct. Lipid A is the toxic lipid component of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS, endotoxin) that forms the outer leaflet of the Gram-negative outer membrane. Gram-positive bacteria have no outer membrane at all, so they have no Lipid A/LPS; Lipid A is therefore a structure unique to the Gram-negative cell envelope and is responsible for much of the systemic toxicity (fever, septic shock) seen in Gram-negative infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A capsule can be present in either Gram-positive (for example pneumococcus) or Gram-negative organisms; it is not restricted to Gram-negatives.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Flagella, when present, occur in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative species; motility is independent of Gram reaction.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Volutin (metachromatic) granules are cytoplasmic storage inclusions seen in organisms such as Corynebacterium diphtheriae, a Gram-positive bacterium, so they are not a Gram-negative-only feature.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Lipid A as the toxic outer-membrane component unique to Gram-negative bacteria, absent from the Gram-positive wall.

field_notes.reuse: Reuses pending concept CON-INF-BF26D7E563FB78 ('The Gram-negative outer membrane carries toxic lipid A and porins that admit only small solutes, not amino acids'), docs/Ain-Shams-Source-Imports/concept/ASU-INF-microbiology-concepts.md, exact match. Article ART-INF-CELL-WALL-OUTER-MEMBRANE confirmed present in the same batch.

questions.title: Flagellar arrangement distributed over the entire bacterial cell
questions.question: Flagella distributed over the entire bacterial cell are known as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Monotrichous describes a single flagellum at one pole of the cell (for example Vibrio cholerae), not flagella covering the whole surface.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lophotrichous describes a tuft of several flagella at one pole, still localised rather than distributed over the entire cell.
explanations.C: Correct. Peritrichous flagellar arrangement means flagella are distributed all around the entire bacterial cell surface rather than confined to one or both poles, giving organisms such as E. coli and Salmonella their characteristic tumbling motility pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Amphitrichous describes a single flagellum (or tuft) at each of the two opposite poles, not all-over distribution.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Conjugative flagella" is not a recognised flagellar-arrangement category; conjugation is a separate process mediated by sex pili, not flagella.

questions.learning_objective: Name peritrichous as the flagellar arrangement in which flagella are distributed over the entire bacterial cell surface.

field_notes.reuse: Reuses pending concept CON-INF-E4E8831D2BE517 ('Bacterial flagellar arrangement is named by position: ... peritrichous'), docs/Assiut-Source-Imports/concept/AUN-INI-105-concepts.md, exact match naming all four arrangements including peritrichous. Article ART-INF-AUN-INI105-BACTERIAL-CELL-STRUCTURE confirmed present in the same batch.

questions.title: Bacterial growth-curve phase correlating with symptomatic illness
questions.question: Which phase of bacterial growth corresponds to period of symptoms and signs?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lag phase, a period of metabolic adaptation with little or no cell division, is more commonly likened to the incubation period of an infection (before symptoms appear), not the symptomatic period itself.
explanations.B: Correct per this bank's printed key. The teaching correlation used here maps the log (exponential) growth phase, when bacterial numbers and toxin/antigen load are rising fastest, to the period of clinical symptoms and signs. (Note: this same stem recurs later in this bank's own cohort-repeat block with a different printed key, C/stationary phase -- see the doubt note.) This growth-curve-to-illness mapping is a teaching mnemonic rather than a strict biological law, which is exactly why different sources can print it with different phase assignments, as this bank's own cohort-repeat shows.
explanations.C: Incorrect per this printed key, though flagged in field_notes as arguably the more standard correlation (stationary phase = plateau of illness/fastigium) -- see the doubt note.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The decline (death) phase, when viable numbers fall, is more commonly likened to the convalescent/recovery period, not the symptomatic peak.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Convalescent phase" is not one of the standard bacterial growth-curve phases (lag, log, stationary, decline); it is a clinical disease-course term being used here as a distractor.

questions.learning_objective: State the teaching correlation between the bacterial growth curve and stages of clinical infection, and recognise this bank's internal key conflict on which phase maps to symptomatic illness.

field_notes.mint: find-existing.mjs run for "bacterial growth curve infection stages symptoms" -- no hit; the closest existing record (CON-INF-6D56F46B5F1EF4, lag vs stationary phase definitions) does not address the growth-curve-to-disease-stage correlation this stem and its Q11 repeat both test, so a new concept was minted rather than overloaded.
field_notes.doubt: AUTHOR DOUBT, not silently resolved: this exact stem recurs at Q11 (p.30) with a DIFFERENT printed key (C, Stationary phase) render-confirmed on both pages. Many teaching schemes actually favour stationary phase = period of illness/fastigium (by analogy: lag=incubation, log=prodrome, stationary=illness, decline=convalescence), which would make Q11's key the textbook-consistent one and this question's key (B, Log phase) the outlier. Per lane convention (first occurrence authored, repeat held), this question keeps its own printed key as authored; Q11 is held as the duplicate, with this conflict noted in its hold reason rather than silently picking a 'winner'.

questions.title: Plasmid type unstable and easily degraded by exonucleases
questions.question: Which plasmid type is unstable and can be easily attacked by exonucleases?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Host range (broad vs narrow) describes how many bacterial species a plasmid can replicate in, not its physical stability against exonucleases.
explanations.B: Incorrect. As with broad host range, narrow host range describes replication compatibility, not resistance to exonuclease attack.
explanations.C: Correct. Most bacterial plasmids are covalently closed circular DNA, which has no free ends for exonucleases to act on and is therefore relatively stable. A linear plasmid, by contrast, has two free DNA ends exposed to the cytoplasm, making it an easy substrate for exonucleases and comparatively unstable -- which is why circular topology is the typical, more stable form.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A shuttle vector is a plasmid engineered to replicate in two different host types (for example bacteria and yeast); this describes function, not the linear-vs-circular structural feature that determines exonuclease vulnerability.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Conjugative plasmids are defined by their ability to mediate their own transfer between cells (carrying transfer/tra genes), not by unusual susceptibility to exonucleases.

questions.learning_objective: Identify linear plasmid topology (as opposed to the typical closed-circular form) as the structurally unstable form vulnerable to exonuclease degradation.

field_notes.mint: find-existing.mjs run for "linear plasmid exonuclease" -- no hit, safe to create.

questions.title: Characteristic feature of viruses
questions.question: Which of the following is a character of viruses?

options.C: Viruses can grow outside host cells.
options.E: The viruses contains both DNA and RNA

explanations.A: Correct. A virus is acellular -- it is not a true cell of any kind (prokaryotic or eukaryotic). It has no independent metabolism, no ribosomes of its own and cannot reproduce outside a host cell, which is the fundamental feature distinguishing it from bacteria and fungi, both of which are genuinely living, independently metabolising cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Viruses are far smaller than the micrometre scale used for bacteria and cells; they are measured in nanometres.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites and cannot grow or replicate outside a living host cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Only some viruses are enveloped (acquiring a lipid envelope from the host cell membrane during budding); many medically important viruses are non-enveloped (naked), so this is not a universal viral character.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A virus contains either DNA or RNA as its genome, never both together.

questions.learning_objective: State that a virus is acellular (not a true cell), distinguishing it from the living, independently metabolising bacterial and fungal cell.

field_notes.reuse: Reuses pending concept CON-INF-E3C75AA9B1F5E5 ('A virus is acellular; fungi and human cells are eukaryotic, bacteria are prokaryotic'), docs/Assiut-Source-Imports/concept/AUN-INI-105-concepts.md, exact match on the acellular fact this stem tests. Article ART-INF-AUN-INI105-BACTERIAL-CELL-STRUCTURE-2 confirmed present in the same batch.

questions.title: Bacterial structure protecting against phagocytosis
questions.question: Which one protects bacterial cell against phagocytosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Peptidoglycan is a structural wall component providing rigidity and shape; it does not itself impede phagocytic uptake.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lipid components such as Lipid A drive inflammatory/toxic effects, not resistance to phagocytic engulfment.
explanations.C: Correct. The bacterial capsule is a major antiphagocytic virulence factor: its slippery polysaccharide (or, in Bacillus anthracis, polypeptide) surface resists engulfment by phagocytes and is used both for organism identification (capsular typing) and in vaccine preparation (e.g. pneumococcal and meningococcal capsular vaccines).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mesosomes are internal cytoplasmic-membrane invaginations, not a surface structure and not linked to phagocytosis resistance.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Exopigment (extracellular pigment) production, such as pyocyanin by Pseudomonas, is a diagnostic/virulence feature unrelated to phagocytosis resistance.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the capsule as the bacterial structure that resists phagocytosis and serves as a virulence factor and vaccine target.

questions.title: Plasmid able to mobilize itself and another plasmid cell-to-cell
questions.question: Which of the following plasmids can mobilize itself and another plasmid from cell to cell?

explanations.A: Correct. A conjugative plasmid carries its own transfer (tra) genes, which build the sex pilus and machinery needed to transfer itself -- and, by mobilisation, other non-conjugative plasmids present in the same donor cell -- into a recipient cell during conjugation. This self-sufficient, high-frequency, wide-host-range transfer ability is the plasmid's defining feature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A shuttle vector is engineered to replicate in two different host organisms (for example bacteria and yeast); this describes replication compatibility, not cell-to-cell mobilisation ability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Broad host range describes how many bacterial species a plasmid can replicate in, not whether it can mobilise itself and other plasmids by conjugation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Artificial plasmid" describes an engineered/laboratory-constructed plasmid, not a category defined by conjugative transfer ability.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Stringent plasmids are maintained at low copy number per cell (as opposed to relaxed plasmids at high copy number); copy-number control is unrelated to conjugative mobilisation ability.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the conjugative plasmid as the type able to mobilize itself, and other plasmids, from cell to cell.

field_notes.reuse: Reuses pending concept CON-INF-29B8D844843328 ('Conjugative plasmids characteristically show a high frequency of transfer, a wide range of hosts, and multiple genetic determinants'), docs/Assiut-Source-Imports/concept/AUN-INI-105-concepts.md, exact match. questions.title: Form of gene transfer mediated by bacteriophage
questions.question: Which of the following forms of gene transfer is mediated by bacteriophage?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Conjugation is mediated by direct cell-to-cell contact through a sex pilus, not by a bacteriophage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mutation is a spontaneous or induced change in the DNA sequence itself, not a mechanism of gene transfer between cells at all.
explanations.C: Correct. Transduction is the form of horizontal gene transfer in which a bacteriophage, during its lytic cycle, accidentally packages a fragment of the donor bacterium's DNA into a phage particle and then injects it into a new recipient cell upon subsequent infection, transferring the donor genes along with it. Because the phage particle, not the bacterium itself, carries the transferred DNA between donor and recipient, transduction can occur even between cells with no direct contact, unlike conjugation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transformation is the direct uptake of free (naked) DNA from the environment by a competent recipient cell; no phage is involved.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Transposition is the movement of a mobile genetic element (transposon/insertion sequence) from one DNA location to another within or between DNA molecules already inside the same cell, not a form of transfer mediated by an external phage.

questions.learning_objective: Identify transduction as the bacteriophage-mediated form of horizontal gene transfer, distinguishing it from conjugation, transformation, mutation and transposition.

field_notes.mint: find-existing.mjs run for "transduction gene transfer phage" and "transduction bacteriophage" -- the closest existing record (CON-INF-E9C14F5981ACE5, 'Generalized transduction can transfer non-transmissible plasmid DNA via a bacteriophage') covers one specific detail of transduction, not the general classification fact this stem and its Q30 repeat test (that transduction, as opposed to conjugation/transformation/mutation/transposition, is THE phage-mediated route) -- minted a new umbrella concept rather than overloading the narrower one; AUN-INI-105's own field_notes independently record the identical search ("bacteriophage" -> no term-defining hit) before minting their own bacteriophage-definition concept, confirming this gap is real, not a search miss.

questions.title: Definition of phoresis as a host-parasite relationship
questions.question: Phoresis is a host parasite relation in which the:

options.D: Parasite is carried by the host.
options.E: Host is resistant to the parasite

explanations.A: Incorrect. Host specificity (a parasite restricted to one host species) is a separate concept from phoresis, which describes a mode of association, not host range.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Phoresis does not involve the host gaining any benefit; that describes mutualism, a different type of relationship.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dependence on the host for nutrition or habitat describes ordinary parasitism generally, not the specific defining feature of phoresis.
explanations.D: Correct. Phoresis is a host-parasite (or organism-organism) relationship in which one organism is simply carried by the other for transport, without deriving nourishment from it and without harming or benefiting the carrier -- a purely mechanical, transport-only association, distinct from true parasitism, commensalism or mutualism. This makes phoresis fundamentally different from parasitism (harm to the host), commensalism (benefit to one side only, no harm) and mutualism (benefit to both), since none of the usual costs or benefits of those relationships apply.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Host resistance describes an immune/defence relationship, not the transport-only association that defines phoresis.

questions.learning_objective: Define phoresis as a transport-only host-parasite association in which the parasite is simply carried by the host, without nourishment, benefit or harm.

field_notes.mint: find-existing.mjs run for "phoresis" and "phoresis host parasite carried" -- the only hits were an unrelated fly-biology record (Dermatobia phoresis, cutaneous myiasis) and unrelated haematology vignettes matching the string "phoresis" inside "electrophoresis"; no record defines phoresis as a host-parasite-relationship term, so a new concept was minted.

questions.title: Fine filamentous appendages arising from basal bodies in Gram-negative bacteria
questions.question: The fine filamentous appendages arising from basal bodies in the cytoplasmic membrane of many Gram-negative bacteria are known as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Flagella are the (comparatively thick, helical) organelles of motility, also anchored by a basal body, but they are distinguished from pili by their larger diameter and motile function rather than adhesive function; this stem's emphasis on fine, non-motile filamentous appendages points to pili instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mesosomes are internal cytoplasmic-membrane invaginations, not external filamentous surface appendages.
explanations.C: Correct. Pili (fimbriae) are fine, hair-like proteinaceous appendages that arise from basal bodies in the cytoplasmic membrane of many Gram-negative bacteria. Ordinary pili mediate adhesion to host cells and surfaces, while specialised sex pili mediate conjugative DNA transfer, but structurally both are the fine filamentous appendages this stem describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plasmids are extrachromosomal circular DNA molecules, not surface appendages at all.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Spores are dormant survival structures formed by certain Gram-positive genera (Bacillus, Clostridium), not filamentous surface appendages of Gram-negative bacteria.

questions.learning_objective: Identify pili (fimbriae) as the fine filamentous appendages arising from basal bodies in the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane, distinct from flagella.

field_notes.mint: find-existing.mjs run for "pili", "pili basal body" and "pili filamentous appendages basal body" -- existing pili records (CON-INF-BC446C9816D9CE ordinary vs sex pili function, CON-INF-1EAFF70A6FC769 pili/flagella and invasion) describe pili FUNCTION, not the structural description (fine filamentous appendages from basal bodies) this stem tests -- minted a new structural-description concept rather than overloading a functional one.

questions.title: Bacterium characterized by exopigment formation
questions.question: Which of the following bacteria is characterized by exopigment formation?

explanations.A: Incorrect. E. coli is not characteristically pigment-producing; it is identified by other biochemical and culture features.
explanations.B: Correct. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is classically characterised by exopigment (extracellular pigment) formation -- most notably pyocyanin, a blue-green pigment diffusible into the surrounding culture medium -- which is a recognised aid to its identification on culture, alongside its oxidase-positive reaction. This pigment production is a practical bedside and laboratory clue: a blue-green tint on a wound dressing or in a culture plate is often the first hint of Pseudomonas infection before formal biochemical confirmation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Serratia is better known for a red pigment (prodigiosin) in some strains, but this is not the exopigment-producing organism this classic teaching stem targets; Pseudomonas is the standard answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus is identified by Gram-positive cocci morphology, catalase and coagulase positivity, not by exopigment formation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Streptococci are identified by haemolysis pattern and Lancefield grouping, not by exopigment formation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the classic exopigment (pyocyanin)-producing bacterium.

questions.title: Gene-transfer method using direct uptake of DNA by the recipient cell
questions.question: Which of the following methods of gene transfer employ direct uptake of DNA by recipient cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Conjugation requires direct cell-to-cell contact via a sex pilus, not free uptake of DNA from the surrounding environment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mutation is a change in existing DNA sequence, not a mechanism by which DNA is transferred between cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transduction requires a bacteriophage vector to carry the DNA into the recipient cell, not direct uptake of naked DNA.
explanations.D: Correct. Transformation is the process in which a competent recipient bacterial cell directly takes up free (naked) DNA released into the environment from another cell, with sufficient homology allowing the incoming DNA to recombine into the recipient's own chromosome. Because it depends on the recipient's own competence machinery rather than an external vector (phage) or direct cell contact, transformation is the gene-transfer route most exploited artificially in the laboratory to introduce plasmid DNA into bacteria.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Transposition is the intracellular relocation of a mobile genetic element within or between DNA molecules already inside one cell, not transfer of DNA between separate cells.

questions.learning_objective: Identify transformation as the gene-transfer method involving direct uptake of free DNA by a competent recipient cell.

questions.title: Correct sequence of the viral replication cycle
questions.question: What is the correct sequence of events in viral replication cycle?

options.A: Attachment - uncoating - penetration - replication - gene expression - assembly - release.
options.B: Attachment - uncoating - penetration - gene expression - replication - assembly - release.
options.C: Attachment - penetration - uncoating - gene expression - replication - assembly - release.
options.D: Penetration - attachment - uncoating - gene expression - replication - assembly - release.
options.E: Penetration - uncoating - attachment - gene expression - replication - assembly - release.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This places uncoating before penetration, but the virus must first penetrate the host cell before its capsid can be removed (uncoated) inside the cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Uncoating cannot precede penetration; the capsid is stripped away after the virus has entered the cell, not before.
explanations.C: Correct. The standard viral replication cycle proceeds: attachment (binding host-cell receptors), penetration (entry into the cell), uncoating (release of the viral genome from its capsid), gene expression, replication (of the genome), assembly (of new virions) and release from the cell. This order -- attach, then penetrate, then uncoat, before genome expression and copying can begin -- is the sequence tested here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Attachment to a host-cell receptor must occur before penetration into the cell, not after it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. As above, attachment (receptor binding) is the necessary first step and cannot follow penetration.

questions.learning_objective: State the correct order of the viral replication cycle: attachment, penetration, uncoating, gene expression/replication, assembly, release.

field_notes.reuse: Reuses pending concept CON-INF-2C32D6BA60368C ('The viral replication cycle proceeds: attachment, penetration, uncoating, replication, assembly, release'), docs/Ain-Shams-Source-Imports/concept/ASU-INF-microbiology-concepts.md. The existing label omits an explicit 'gene expression' step between uncoating and replication that this stem's own options separate out; the underlying ordering (attach->penetrate->uncoat->[express/replicate]->assemble->release) is identical, so this is treated as the same taught sequence rather than a conflicting one. Article ART-INF-VIRAL-CULTURE-DETECTION-ENTRY-REPLICATION confirmed present in the same batch.

questions.title: Feature of insertion sequence elements
questions.question: Insertion sequence elements:

options.B: Carry virulence and transposition genes in its central piece.
options.C: Have examples as Tn5 and Tn7.
options.D: Have direct or inverted repeats at their ends.
options.E: Are the most complex form of transposable elements.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Insertion sequences are the simplest transposable elements, carrying only the transposase gene needed for their own movement; they do not carry accessory genes such as antibiotic resistance.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Carrying extra genes such as virulence or additional determinants in a central region flanked by insertion sequences describes a composite transposon, not a plain insertion sequence itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tn5 and Tn7 are named (composite/complex) transposons, not insertion sequences; insertion sequences are simpler elements typically named IS followed by a number (e.g. IS1).
explanations.D: Correct. Insertion sequence elements are the simplest mobile genetic elements: a central transposase gene flanked at both ends by short direct or inverted repeat sequences, which are the recognition sites the transposase acts on to mobilise the element. Because it carries no genes beyond the one needed for its own movement, an insertion sequence contributes to genome plasticity and mutagenesis (by inserting into and disrupting genes) without itself conferring any new phenotype such as resistance.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Insertion sequences are the SIMPLEST, not the most complex, transposable elements; composite and complex transposons (built from two insertion sequences flanking extra genes) are more elaborate.

questions.learning_objective: State that insertion sequence elements are the simplest transposable elements, carrying only a transposase gene flanked by direct or inverted repeats.

questions.title: Most common physical form of bacterial plasmids
questions.question: The most common form of plasmids is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Linear plasmids exist (for example in some Borrelia and Streptomyces species) but are the exception, not the typical form, and are comparatively unstable to exonuclease attack.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Semicircular" is not a recognised plasmid topology.
explanations.C: Incorrect, as the more precise answer. Plasmids are indeed circular, but 'circular' alone does not capture the specific, most-common supercoiled topology this stem is testing -- see option D.
explanations.D: Correct. The most common and typical form of a bacterial plasmid is covalently closed circular (CCC) double-stranded DNA: a closed loop with no free ends, usually supercoiled, which protects it from exonuclease degradation and is the standard state in which plasmids exist and are purified in the laboratory. This closed-loop, usually supercoiled state is also what makes plasmid DNA separable from linear chromosomal DNA fragments by standard laboratory techniques such as gel electrophoresis and alkaline lysis plasmid preparation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Square" is not a real DNA topology and does not apply to plasmids.

questions.learning_objective: Identify covalently closed circular (CCC) DNA as the most common physical form of a bacterial plasmid.

questions.title: Defining characteristic of the viral envelope
questions.question: The viral envelope is characterized by:

options.C: Being made up of subunits called capsomers.
options.D: Making the virus more resistant to phagocytosis.
options.E: Presence in all types of viruses.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Symmetry (icosahedral, helical or complex) is a property of the capsid/nucleocapsid, not conferred by the envelope.
explanations.B: Correct. The viral envelope is lipoprotein in nature: a lipid bilayer derived from the host cell membrane during budding, studded with virus-encoded glycoprotein spikes, wrapped around the nucleocapsid. Because it is host-derived, the envelope also carries some host membrane proteins alongside the virus's own glycoprotein spikes, and it is disrupted by lipid solvents and detergents, a property exploited by alcohol-based disinfectants against enveloped viruses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Capsomers are the protein subunits that build the capsid, not the envelope.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An envelope generally makes a virus LESS resistant to environmental stress (e.g. drying, detergents, disinfectants) than a naked (non-enveloped) virus, not more resistant to phagocytosis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Not all viruses are enveloped; many medically important viruses (for example poliovirus, adenovirus) are naked/non-enveloped, so envelope presence is not universal.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the viral envelope as a lipoprotein structure derived from the host cell membrane, distinct from the capsid's protein/capsomer composition.

questions.title: Fungi able to grow as mycelium or as yeast depending on temperature
questions.question: Fungi that can grow as mycelium or as yeast on temperature variation, are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Thermally active" is not the standard term for this behaviour; it does not specifically describe the mould-to-yeast conversion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Opportunistic describes fungi that cause disease chiefly in immunocompromised hosts, a separate classification from the temperature-dependent morphology switch this stem asks about.
explanations.C: Correct. Thermally dimorphic fungi grow as a filamentous mould (mycelium) at ambient/room temperature (in the environment) and convert to a yeast (or yeast-like) form at body temperature in vivo -- the classic examples being Histoplasma, Blastomyces and Coccidioides. Correct identification of thermal dimorphism matters clinically: a mycology laboratory culturing a suspected dimorphic fungus at 37°C versus room temperature can see the morphology switch directly, which is itself a diagnostic test.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Thermally variable" is not the recognised term; the correct term for this specific mould-yeast temperature switch is thermally dimorphic.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Saprophytic describes fungi that live on dead organic matter, an ecological/nutritional classification unrelated to the temperature-dependent morphology switch tested here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify thermal dimorphism as the fungal property of growing as mould at ambient temperature and as yeast at body temperature.

field_notes.reuse: Reuses pending concept CON-INF-44400FF4328CA8 ('Dimorphic fungi grow as a mold in nature/room temperature and as a yeast in vivo/body temperature'), docs/Ain-Shams-Source-Imports/concept/ASU-INF-microbiology-concepts.md, exact match. questions.title: Function of the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane
questions.question: Which of the following is a function of cytoplasmic membrane?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adhesion is chiefly mediated by surface appendages such as pili/fimbriae, not the cytoplasmic membrane itself.
explanations.B: Correct. Because bacteria lack mitochondria, the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation take place across the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane instead, making it functionally analogous to the inner mitochondrial membrane of a eukaryotic cell -- a key cytoplasmic-membrane function. This membrane-based electron transport chain generates the proton-motive force the bacterium uses for ATP synthesis, active transport and (in motile species) powering flagellar rotation, making the cytoplasmic membrane functionally indispensable rather than a simple passive barrier.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Gram staining reaction is determined by the cell WALL (peptidoglycan thickness and outer membrane presence), not the cytoplasmic membrane beneath it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Motility is produced by flagella, external organelles anchored in, but not equivalent to, the cytoplasmic membrane's own function.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Conjugation is mediated by sex pili and is a whole-cell process of DNA transfer, not a direct function performed by the cytoplasmic membrane itself.

questions.learning_objective: Identify electron transport (oxidative phosphorylation) as a function of the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane, given the absence of mitochondria.

questions.title: Flagella compared with fimbria
questions.question: Compared with fimbria, flagella is:

explanations.A: Correct. Flagella are typically few in number per cell (one to a modest tuft, depending on arrangement), whereas fimbriae/pili are numerous, often several hundred per cell -- a useful distinguishing feature between the two types of bacterial surface appendage alongside their different functions (motility vs adhesion). These differences in number, thickness, length and shape reflect the two structures' different jobs: a cell typically needs only a few flagella to swim efficiently, but many pili to maximise adhesive contact with a surface or host cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Flagella are helical/wavy structures that rotate to produce movement, not straight; pili/fimbriae are the straighter, more rigid appendages.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Flagella are thicker in diameter than fimbriae/pili, not thinner.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Flagella are typically longer than fimbriae/pili, not shorter.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Flagella are the organelles OF motility (rotating to drive movement); "non-motile chains" describes neither flagella nor the fimbria comparison this stem asks about.

questions.subtopic: Bacterial cell structure — flagella vs fimbriae
questions.learning_objective: Compare flagella with fimbriae/pili: flagella are few in number, thicker, longer and helical, while fimbriae are numerous, thinner, shorter and straighter.

questions.title: The 'infectious part' of a virus
questions.question: Which parts of the virus act as an 'infectious part'?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Capsomers are structural protein subunits of the capsid; they protect and package the genome but are not themselves the infectious agent.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Envelope glycoprotein spikes mediate host-cell receptor attachment for enveloped viruses, but this is an entry step, not the infectious component itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lipoproteins make up the envelope, a protective/entry structure, not the genetic material that actually initiates infection.
explanations.D: Correct. The viral nucleic acid (the genome, DNA or RNA) is the truly infectious part of the virus: it alone carries the genetic information needed to direct the host cell's machinery to produce new virions, and purified viral nucleic acid, introduced into a susceptible cell, can in some cases initiate a full infectious cycle even without the rest of the virion. This is why, for some non-enveloped viruses, experimentally purified nucleic acid alone (stripped of its capsid) can still be infectious when introduced directly into a susceptible cell, even though it is far less efficient than a complete virion using its normal attachment and entry machinery.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Viral antigens are the immunogenic surface molecules recognised by the host immune system; they are not what makes the virus infectious.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the viral nucleic acid (genome) as the infectious component of the virus, as distinct from its structural capsid/envelope proteins.

questions.title: Mode of fungal reproduction
questions.question: How do fungi reproduce?

options.B: Spore formation which may be sexual or asexual.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Binary fission is a bacterial mode of reproduction, not the characteristic fungal one.
explanations.B: Correct. Fungi characteristically reproduce by spore formation, and fungal spores may be produced either sexually (following fusion of compatible mating types, generating genetic recombination) or asexually (mitotically, producing clonal spores) -- this dual sexual/asexual spore-forming capacity is the defining reproductive feature of fungi. This dual capability lets fungi both generate genetic diversity through sexual spores when conditions favour it and propagate rapidly and clonally through asexual spores when they do not, giving the fungal life cycle considerable flexibility.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hyphal fragmentation can occasionally propagate a fungal colony but is not the characteristic, defining reproductive mechanism (spore formation is).
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Formation of a unicellular cell" is not a recognised fungal reproductive mechanism.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Mitotic division alone describes ordinary somatic/vegetative growth, not the spore-based sexual-or-asexual reproductive cycle that defines fungal reproduction.

questions.learning_objective: State that fungi reproduce by spore formation, which may occur either sexually or asexually.

field_notes.mint: find-existing.mjs run for "fungi sexual asexual spore" and "fungi reproduce" -- the closest existing record (CON-INF-2FEBA5328F9E83, 'Fungal spores are an essential part of the fungal life cycle, unlike bacterial survival spores') addresses spores generally versus bacterial survival spores, not the sexual-vs-asexual reproductive-mode distinction this stem tests -- minted a new, more specific concept rather than overloading the general one.

questions.title: Defining feature of specific parasites
questions.question: Which of the following describes specific parasites?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Accidentally acquired" describes an accidental parasite (one that infects an unusual, non-typical host by chance), a different classification from host specificity.
explanations.B: Correct. A specific parasite is one that is restricted to, and can complete its life cycle only in, a single host species; this narrow host range (as opposed to non-specific/euryxenous parasites that can infect multiple host species) is what defines specificity. Host specificity has practical consequences for transmission and control, since a specific parasite cannot simply spread to a new host species the way a non-specific (multi-host) parasite can if its one required host becomes unavailable.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Anthropozoonotic describes a zoonosis transmissible from animals to humans, a transmission-direction classification, not host specificity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Free-living describes an organism that does not require a host at all, the opposite of being a parasite.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Zooanthroponotic describes transmission from humans to animals, again a transmission-direction classification rather than host specificity.

questions.learning_objective: Define a specific parasite as one restricted to a single host species, distinguishing host specificity from zoonotic transmission-direction terms.

field_notes.mint: find-existing.mjs run for "specific parasite host" and "host specific parasite" -- no hit, safe to create.

questions.title: Identifying a primary lymphoid organ
questions.question: Which of the following is a primary lymphoid organ?

explanations.A: Correct. Bone marrow, together with the thymus, is a primary (central) lymphoid organ: the site where lymphocytes are generated and complete their initial development and maturation (B cells in the bone marrow itself, T-cell precursors continuing on to mature in the thymus), before circulating to secondary lymphoid tissue to encounter antigen. Only after this initial generation and maturation step in a primary lymphoid organ do naive lymphocytes leave to populate the secondary (peripheral) lymphoid organs -- lymph nodes, spleen and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue such as Peyer's patches and tonsils -- where they actually encounter antigen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lymph node is a secondary (peripheral) lymphoid organ, where mature lymphocytes encounter antigen and mount an immune response, not where they are generated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Peyer's patches are secondary lymphoid tissue in the gut wall (part of MALT), a site of antigen encounter, not lymphocyte generation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ that filters blood and mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The tonsil is secondary lymphoid tissue (part of MALT) involved in antigen encounter in the oropharynx, not lymphocyte generation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify bone marrow (with the thymus) as a primary lymphoid organ, as distinct from the secondary lymphoid organs (lymph node, spleen, Peyer's patches, tonsil).

questions.subject: imm

questions.title: Lineage classification of natural killer cells
questions.question: Natural killer cells are members of which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Basophils are a granulocyte lineage distinct from lymphocytes, involved in allergic/immediate hypersensitivity reactions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Eosinophils are a granulocyte lineage associated with allergy and parasitic infection, not the lymphocyte lineage.
explanations.C: Correct. The functional classes of lymphocytes are T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes and natural killer (NK) cells; despite lacking the antigen-specific receptors of T and B cells, NK cells are classified as a third lymphocyte lineage, part of the innate rather than adaptive arm of lymphoid immunity. Unlike T and B lymphocytes, NK cells do not carry antigen-specific receptors and act as part of innate rather than adaptive immunity, but their shared lymphoid morphology and lineage place them in the same functional lymphocyte category.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Monocytes are the blood precursor of macrophages, part of the mononuclear phagocyte lineage, not lymphocytes.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Neutrophils are a granulocyte lineage specialised for phagocytosis of bacteria, not lymphocytes.

questions.subtopic: Immunology — cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: Classify natural killer (NK) cells as a lymphocyte lineage, alongside T and B lymphocytes.

questions.subject: imm

questions.title: The professional antigen-presenting cell type
questions.question: Which one of the following cell types act as professional antigen presenting cells?

explanations.A: Incorrect. T lymphocytes are the cells that RECEIVE antigen presented to them, expressing the T-cell receptor; they are not themselves classed as professional antigen-presenting cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mast cells mediate immediate hypersensitivity via histamine release; they are not a professional antigen-presenting cell type.
explanations.C: Correct. Dendritic cells are the antigen-presenting cell best suited to capture antigen in peripheral tissue, migrate to lymphoid organs, and present it via MHC to activate naive T lymphocytes, making them the prototypical professional antigen-presenting cell (alongside macrophages and B cells). Their unique capacity to prime a naive T cell (one that has never encountered its antigen before) is what earns dendritic cells the title of the most 'professional' antigen-presenting cell, ahead of macrophages and B cells, which are more effective at presenting to already-primed T cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plasma cells are terminally differentiated, antibody-secreting B cells; they are not classed among the professional antigen-presenting cells.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Natural killer cells are innate cytotoxic lymphocytes, not antigen-presenting cells.

questions.learning_objective: Identify dendritic cells as the professional antigen-presenting cell best suited to activate naive T lymphocytes.

questions.subject: imm

questions.title: The arm of the immune system producing a rapid non-specific response
questions.question: Which of the following can produce rapid non-specific immune response?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The adaptive immune system is slower to respond on first exposure (days) and is antigen-specific, the opposite of the rapid, non-specific response this stem asks about.
explanations.B: Correct. Innate immunity responds rapidly, non-specifically and to the same degree on every exposure (it does not improve with repeat exposure, unlike adaptive immunity), making it the body's first line of defence before an antigen-specific adaptive response can develop. This is the key trade-off with adaptive immunity, which is antigen-specific and improves with repeated exposure (memory) but takes days to mount on a first encounter, whereas innate immunity is ready immediately, every time.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leukocytes is too broad a category (it includes both innate cells like neutrophils and adaptive cells like lymphocytes), not a specific description of the rapid, non-specific arm of immunity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lymphatic system is an anatomical circulatory/drainage system for lymph and immune cells, not itself a description of the rapid non-specific immune response.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Memory response is a feature of adaptive immunity's SECOND exposure, which is faster and stronger, not the same on every exposure -- the opposite of what this stem describes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the innate immune system as the arm producing a rapid, non-specific response that does not vary in strength between exposures.

questions.subject: imm

questions.title: Receptors phagocytes use to recognize microbes in blood
questions.question: What is used by phagocytes to recognize microbes in blood?

explanations.A: Incorrect. B-cell receptors are the antigen-specific surface immunoglobulin used by B lymphocytes, not the pattern-recognition receptors used by phagocytes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Killer-activating receptors are used by natural killer cells to trigger cytotoxicity, not by phagocytes to recognise microbes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Killer-inhibitory receptors are also an NK-cell receptor type (recognising self MHC class I to prevent killing of healthy cells), not a phagocyte microbe-recognition receptor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. T-cell receptors are the antigen-specific receptors of T lymphocytes, requiring antigen presentation on MHC, not the direct pattern-recognition receptors phagocytes use.
explanations.E: Correct. Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are pattern-recognition receptors on innate immune cells, including phagocytes, that directly recognise conserved pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, such as bacterial LPS or flagellin) on microbes, triggering their recognition and subsequent phagocytosis and activation. Because TLRs recognise broad, conserved microbial patterns rather than any one specific antigen, they let phagocytes respond to a wide range of pathogens immediately, without needing prior sensitisation the way an antigen-specific adaptive receptor would.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Toll-like receptors as the pattern-recognition receptors phagocytes use to recognise microbial PAMPs.

The existing label names PRRs generically; Toll-like receptors are the classic, most commonly taught PRR family and are treated here as the same fact this stem is testing at the specific-example level, not a conflicting one. questions.title: Cell type that migrates to the thymus for maturation
questions.question: Which of the following cells go to thymus for maturation?

explanations.A: Incorrect. B cells complete their maturation in the bone marrow itself; the bone marrow performs haematopoiesis and B-cell maturation, but not T-cell maturation, so B cells do not need to migrate to the thymus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Erythrocytes (red blood cells) mature in the bone marrow and do not require thymic processing at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Haematopoietic stem cells reside in and give rise to all blood lineages from the bone marrow; the thymus receives only committed T-lineage precursors, not the multipotent stem cell itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Natural killer cells develop largely independent of the thymus and are not the classic thymus-dependent maturing lineage this stem tests.
explanations.E: Correct. T-cell precursors leave the bone marrow and travel to the thymus, where they undergo maturation and selection (positive and negative selection against self-antigens) before emerging as mature, self-tolerant T lymphocytes -- the defining reason the thymus is a primary lymphoid organ. This thymic education step, absent for B cells, is precisely why the thymus (with the bone marrow) is classed as a primary lymphoid organ and why T-cell but not B-cell development depends on it.

questions.learning_objective: Identify T cells as the lymphocyte lineage that completes maturation in the thymus, as distinct from B cells maturing in the bone marrow.

questions.title: Defining function of natural killer (NK) cells
questions.question: Which of the following describes Natural Killer (NK) cells?

options.D: They kill tumour and virus-infected cells.

explanations.A: Incorrect. NK cells are a distinct lymphocyte lineage from B cells, part of innate rather than humoral adaptive immunity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. NK cells are innate lymphocytes that kill without needing prior antigen-specific sensitisation, unlike cytotoxic (CD8+) T cells, which are adaptive and antigen-specific.
explanations.C: Incorrect. NK cell activity is not characteristically decreased by immunization; immunization chiefly boosts adaptive (T- and B-cell) memory responses.
explanations.D: Correct. Natural killer cells play a key innate role in extracellular killing of virally infected cells and tumour cells, recognising and eliminating cells that have downregulated MHC class I or display stress signals, without requiring prior sensitisation. Because this killing does not require prior antigen exposure or MHC-restricted recognition the way cytotoxic T-cell killing does, NK cells provide an early innate defence against infected or transformed cells before an adaptive cytotoxic response has had time to develop.
explanations.E: Incorrect. NK cells kill target cells directly via cytotoxic granules (perforin/granzymes), not by phagocytosis; phagocytosis is a function of macrophages and neutrophils, not NK cells.

questions.subtopic: Immunology — cells of the immune system
questions.learning_objective: Identify NK cells' defining function as extracellular killing of virally infected cells and tumour cells.

questions.title: Reason viruses are obligate intracellular parasites
questions.question: The cause of viruses being obligate intracellular is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bacteria also lack flagella in many species without being obligate intracellular, so flagellar absence is not the reason viruses must live inside a host cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Genome size varies enormously between viruses (from a few genes to hundreds); a small genome alone does not force an obligate intracellular lifestyle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lack of ATP production is closely related to option E but is not, on its own, the standard textbook phrasing of why viruses are obligate intracellular; the classic reason given is the inability to make their own proteins.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Viruses have no organelles at all (mitochondria included), but the specific, classically taught reason for their obligate intracellular status is protein synthesis dependence, not organelle absence per se.
explanations.E: Correct. Viruses have no ribosomes or translation machinery of their own and so cannot synthesise their own proteins; they multiply only by hijacking a living host cell's ribosomes and tRNA to translate viral mRNA into viral proteins, which is precisely why viruses are obligate intracellular parasites. Because it has no ribosomes, no tRNA and no amino-acid-charging enzymes of its own, a virus is entirely dependent on hijacking a living host cell's translation apparatus to convert its genetic message into functional viral proteins, which is the root cause of its obligate intracellular lifestyle.

questions.learning_objective: State that viruses are obligate intracellular parasites because they lack their own ribosomes/translation machinery and must use the host cell's to synthesise viral proteins.

questions.title: Role of the macrophage during the natural (innate) immune response
questions.question: What is the role of the macrophage during natural immune response?

options.C: Kills the virus-infected cells by perforins and granzymes.
options.D: Kills tumor cells by perforins and granzymes.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Activating plasma cells is not a direct macrophage role; plasma cells arise from activated B cells, chiefly with T-cell (not macrophage) help.
explanations.B: Correct. During the innate (natural) immune response, the macrophage's core role is phagocytosis: it ingests and destroys the antigen/microbe through recognition, engulfment and intracellular killing, in addition to secondary roles in antigen presentation and cytokine production. This phagocytic role sits alongside the macrophage's secondary functions of presenting captured antigen to T cells and secreting cytokines that recruit and activate other immune cells, but ingestion and destruction of the antigen itself is the core innate-response function this question asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Killing via perforins and granzymes is the mechanism used by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells, not macrophages, which kill by phagocytosis rather than granule-mediated cytotoxicity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. As above, perforin/granzyme-mediated tumour cell killing is an NK-cell/cytotoxic-T-cell mechanism, not a macrophage one.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Making specific antibody is a B-cell (plasma cell) function of adaptive humoral immunity, not a macrophage role in the innate response.

questions.learning_objective: Identify phagocytosis (ingesting and destroying the antigen) as the macrophage's core role in the innate immune response.
